deity_of.label: is the God of
deity_of.notes:
The formula "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exod 3:6, 3:15, Matt 22:32, Mark 12:26, Acts 7:32), and "the God of Israel" wherever the corpus uses it.
Added because `spoken_of_as` was carrying it and should not have been. That type means the text applies the name or nature of one to another, and it reads as equivalence -- `god -is spoken of as-> abraham` says, to anyone looking at the graph, that Abraham is a name given to God. Every other edge of that type has a deity at both ends, which is what it is for; this one had a patriarch, and the label made a claim nobody wrote.
It is a relationship and not an identification, which is the whole distinction. Note that Jesus argues the resurrection out of the tense of this very formula at Matthew 22:32 -- "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living" -- so the relationship is load-bearing in the corpus and deserves to be visible as one.

self_designated_as.label: calls himself
self_designated_as.notes:
A title the speaker applies to himself, as against one the text or another speaker applies to him. `titled` cannot carry the difference and the difference is often the entire point.
Exodus 3:14 is the case it exists for: "I AM THAT I AM" is first person, and the next clause sends Moses with "I AM hath sent me unto you" -- the name is given by its bearer. John 8:58 is the other: "Before Abraham was, I am", said by Jesus of himself, after which 8:59 has them take up stones.
**Records who said it, not what follows from it.** Whether the second is a claim to be the first is the oldest argument in the corpus, and this type deliberately stops short of it: it says the words were self-applied in both places and leaves the inference where it belongs. Note also that the KJV supplies "he" at John 8:24, 13:19 and 18:5-6 -- "I am he" -- and does not at 8:58, which is a fact about this translation that a reader weighing the two should have.

spoken_of_as.label: is spoken of as
spoken_of_as.inverse: is a name the text gives to
spoken_of_as.group: What the text says of them
spoken_of_as.notes:
The text applies the name or the nature of one to another. **Not "is".** The whole claim the edge makes is that a particular verse says a particular thing, and the note carries the words.
This is deliberately the humblest type in the vocabulary, because it holds the most contested material in the corpus. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God" (John 1:1) is an edge; so is Thomas's "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), and the Father addressing the Son as God at Hebrews 1:8. The graph records that the corpus says these things and does not conclude anything from them.
Every edge points at whichever record the verse actually names -- `god` where it says God, `the_father` where it says Father -- so that the pattern is visible rather than asserted. Normalising them onto one node would erase the distinction the corpus draws.

quoted.label: quoted
quoted.notes:
One speaker taking another's words. "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Matt 22:32) is Exodus 3:6; "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Matt 22:39) is Leviticus 19:18.
**The corpus quotes far more often than it attributes.** Matthew 22 has four Old Testament citations and names no book for any of them, which is why `bibleont.citations` exists as an analysis. This type is for the cases worth holding as edges -- where the quoting is itself the act, and a reader following the speaker should find the source.
Point it at the person the corpus credits, not at the book: Jesus quotes Moses and David because that is how the corpus speaks of those texts. Where no person is credited, the citation layer is the better home and no edge belongs here.

named_with.label: is named with
named_with.group: What the text says of them
named_with.notes:
The corpus names them together in one formula. "Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19); "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2Cor 13:14).
Neither `spoken_of_as` nor `distinguished_from` fits, and that is the point: **these verses are cited by both sides and do both things at once.** Matthew 28:19 names three and puts them under one singular "name". A type that resolved that would be the graph joining the argument.
**"Formula" was too narrow, and Ephesians 3:14-19 is why.** That passage names all three in a single sentence -- "the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" (v14), "his Spirit" (v16), "that Christ may dwell in your hearts" (v17), "the fulness of God" (v19) -- and it is a prayer rather than a set phrase. Excluding it on register would have been a rule about liturgical style masquerading as a rule about evidence.
It is arguably the stronger case of the three, and the note on those edges says so. The two formulas put the three in parallel and leave the relation between them unstated; the prayer states one -- the Father grants, by the Spirit, so that Christ may dwell. **What that implies is exactly what this type still refuses to say.** Recording that the sentence relates them is not deciding how, and the reader has the verse.

distinguished_from.label: is distinguished from
distinguished_from.group: What the text says of them
distinguished_from.notes:
The text sets two of them apart. "The Father is greater than I" (John 14:28); "No one knows about that day or hour ... nor the Son, but only the Father" (Mark 13:32); "the head of Christ is God" (1Cor 11:3).
**This type exists so the graph cannot lean by omission.** Recording only the verses that join them would make the graph an argument for one reading, and the joining and separating statements sit between the same pair on purpose: John 10:30 and John 14:28 are both edges from Jesus to the Father. That pair *is* the argument as the corpus presents it.
Where a verse is read by one tradition as describing Christ incarnate and by another as describing the eternal relation, the edge records the statement and the note records the wording. It does not resolve which.

put_away.label: sent away
put_away.notes: The text's own word for the dissolution at Ezra 10:19 -- "They pledged to send their wives away" (the Hebrew is "to send out", as at 10:3). Kept as the text puts it rather than translated into divorce, which carries later legal freight the verse does not. (Labelled "put away" until 2026-10-02, the KJV's wording; the type keeps its id.)

accused.label: accused
accused.notes: Where the text uses the word: the Chaldeans accused the Jews (Dan 3:8), the men who accused Daniel and were cast into the den themselves (Dan 6:24), the chief priests accusing Jesus of many things (Mark 15:3). 37 verses carry it. Distinct from `conspired_against`, which is a plot rather than a charge laid, and from `judged`, which is the verdict and not the complaint.

charged.label: charged
charged.notes: A binding instruction laid on someone: "Mordecai had instructed her not to do so" (Esth 2:10), Abimelech warning all the people on pain of death (Gen 26:11). Weaker than a command from God and stronger than a request.

besought.label: pleaded with
besought.notes: Asking, where the text marks it as entreaty rather than conversation: "Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife" (Gen 25:21). The politeness particle (Hebrew נָא, "please") is not this and is deliberately excluded -- a manner of speaking, not an act. (Labelled "besought" until 2026-10-02; the type keeps its id.)

rebuked.label: rebuked
rebuked.notes:
69 verses. Peter rebuking Jesus and being rebuked in turn (Mark 8:32-33) is the pattern: a reproof the narrative reports, not an inference from tone.
**The epistles need a sharper form of that rule, because there the rebuke is often not inferred at all.** 1 Corinthians 5 condemns a named situation at length and explicitly; nothing is being read between the lines. It still gets no edge, because Paul is not describing a confrontation, he is conducting one, and the letter never reports how it ended. Galatians 2:11 is the opposite and does get one: "When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face" -- two named parties, a place, and a completed action, narrated after the fact by one of them.
So: **a document that performs an act is not a document that reports one.** Where the letter rebukes, extract the people involved and leave the congregation out of it; an edge from the writer to the recipients would make every addressee a hub by volume of correspondence and assert an outcome the text withholds.

warned.label: warned
warned.notes: Most of them consequential: Elisha warning the king of Israel of ambushes (2Kgs 6:10), the Magi and then Joseph "warned in a dream" (Matt 2:12, 2:22).

told.label: told
told.notes: Who gave the picture -- spoke the parable, dreamed the dream, saw the vision. Distinct from who wrote it down, which the graph does not record: every "I am" saying in John is Jesus speaking and John reporting, and the figure belongs to the speaker.

explained.label: explained
explained.notes: Who gave the interpretation. Kept apart from `told` because the two are often different people and the difference is the story: Pharaoh dreams and Joseph interprets, Nebuchadnezzar dreams and Daniel interprets, John sees and an angel explains. Where they are the same -- Jesus tells the parable of the tares and explains it in the same chapter -- both edges are recorded and the sameness is visible rather than assumed.

sent.label: sent
sent.notes:
Who sent whom, where the text narrates it. Jacob sent messengers to Esau (Gen 32:3), Ezra sent to Iddo at Casiphia (Ezra 8:17), the Father sends the Comforter (John 14:26) and Jesus sends him too (John 16:7).
**This type exists because of what it lets the graph decline to say.** The Spirit is named by relation to the other two throughout -- "the Spirit of Christ" (Rom 8:9), "the Spirit of his Son" (Gal 4:6), "the Spirit of God" -- and that genitive is unspecified in the text and contested outside it. Sending is the same relationship stated as an act, with named parties and a verse, and recording it gives a reader everything the genitives point at while the graph says nothing about what the three are to one another.

assumed_form_of.label: was a form assumed by
assumed_form_of.notes:
A form deliberately taken and later set aside, where the TEXT narrates the taking. Philippians 2:6-8 is the clearest case and the reason this type exists: "existing in the form of God ... taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness", followed at 2:9 by the exaltation that ends the arrangement. The passage is about the transition, so recording it is reporting rather than interpreting.
Expect it to be rare and expect most candidates to be inferences rather than statements. The angel of the LORD in the flame (Exod 3:2-4), the man who wrestles Jacob (Gen 32:24-30), the captain of the host who accepts worship (Josh 5:13-15) and the fourth figure in the furnace (Dan 3:25) are all readings the text permits and does not make -- mark them `conjectured` and let the corpus argue them.
Melchizedek is the case to be most careful with. Hebrews 7:3 says he is "like the Son of God", which is a comparison whose writer chose a word that stops short of identifying him. Recording him here would have the graph asserting what Hebrews declines to assert.

appeared_to.label: appeared to
appeared_to.notes: A visitation the text narrates: Gabriel sent to Zacharias and to Mary (Luke 1:19, 1:26), to Daniel (Dan 8:16), and Jesus met on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3-5). Recorded as what the text says happened, without classifying it -- vision, dream and bodily appearance are distinctions the text sometimes draws and sometimes does not, and the note carries the wording where it matters.

party_to.label: is party to
party_to.notes: Who the text says the covenant was made with, in the verse that says it.

token_of.label: is the sign of
token_of.notes: The sign the text names: the rainbow in the clouds (Gen 9:13), circumcision (Gen 17:11) -- "a sign of the covenant", in the text's own word -- and "the blood of the covenant" splattered on the people (Exod 24:8). (Labelled "is the token of", the KJV's word, until 2026-10-02; the type keeps its id.)

supersedes.label: makes obsolete
supersedes.notes: Recorded only where the text says so. Heb 8:13 -- "By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete" -- and Jer 31:32, which sets the new one against "the covenant I made with their fathers". The relation exists because those verses exist, not as a scheme laid over the others.

assessed_as.label: did
assessed_as.notes: The formula Kings and Chronicles pronounce on nearly every reign -- "did evil in the sight of the LORD" (1Kgs 15:26), "did what was right in the eyes of the LORD" (15:11) -- with eyes and sight used interchangeably. This is the text's own classification and not a reading of it, which is why the verdict is an entity a reader can stand on and see the whole class from.

described_as.label: is described as
described_as.notes: What the text says the subject is, or is like: an age, a state, a trait, a role, or a verdict on the subject itself. Not a deed -- "did evil in the sight of the LORD" is assessed_as.

titled.label: is called
titled.notes: A name the text gives, in the verse that gives it: "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Rev 5:5), "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29), "I am the true vine" (John 15:1). The title is its own entity, never the creature or object it is built from -- that separation is what keeps one word from meaning both Christ and the devil.

ascribed_to.label: is ascribed to
ascribed_to.notes: The superscription as printed, never authorship. Do not add it where the text does not carry one, and do not infer it from style or subject.

part_of.label: is part of
part_of.notes: Structural containment within the corpus. Transitive, so the validator may drop a direct edge that a path of the same type already implies -- within this type only, since a `speaks_of` edge over the same pair is a different claim and survives.

spoken_in.label: is spoken in
spoken_in.notes: Grouping across taxonomies, grounded verse by verse; the count of shared verses is in the note.

specializes.label: is a narrower form of
specializes.notes: Form to broader form. Never occurrence to form -- that is instance_of. The taxonomy is the graph's reading rather than the text's, so mark it implied unless a verse states the kinship.

instance_of.label: is an instance of
instance_of.notes: Group by form, not by meaning. Two passages sharing a shape may be about entirely different things, and saying they rhyme is not saying they agree.

re_enacts.label: re-enacts
re_enacts.notes: The later account to the earlier. Graded by its evidence, and the note quotes the words that ground it; a link resting on correspondence alone is conjectured and says so.

takes_up.label: takes up the words of
takes_up.inverse: has its words taken up in
takes_up.group: Takes up the words of an earlier account
takes_up.notes: The later account to the earlier whose words it quotes, summarises or gathers. The pairs on the card are the evidence; no likeness between persons is claimed.

same_steps_as.label: has the same steps as
same_steps_as.notes: The later account to the earlier. The pairs on the card are the evidence, quoted from both texts; not a claim that one was told with the other in mind.

possibly_same_as.label: may be the same person as
possibly_same_as.inverse: may be the same person as
possibly_same_as.notes: Two records the text never joins, which a reader holds may be one person. The note gives what points each way; neither record's verses are moved.

occasion_of.label: is an occasion of
occasion_of.group: An occasion of a significant number
occasion_of.notes: The event to the significant number its verses count as a span (forty days, forty years). Cited to those verses; claims no meaning.

composed_of.label: is built from the words
composed_of.notes: Lexical composition only. Never use it to justify a semantic claim, and never emit it alongside is_a reasoning -- if a relation of meaning seems to hold, that is a question for a person, not an edge.

draws_on.label: draws on the image of
draws_on.notes:
**A lexical claim and nothing more.** The title is built on that word; Revelation never says why a lion, and this does not either. "The lion symbolises Christ" would be the reading rather than the text, and is not what this records.
The label is the image's. Into anything that is not an image -- a person, a place, a being, another saying -- it reads "draws on" and "is drawn on by" (`plain_label`, `plain_inverse`). The targets above were widened one at a time and the label never was, so Matthew 1:17 "drew on the image of" Babylon (the 2026-10-02 evaluation; 270 of 489 edges).

drawn_from.label: is drawn from
drawn_from.notes:
Joins the word used as an image to the tangible thing of the same name, where the graph holds one. The lion of 1 Peter 5:8 and the lion Daniel was shut in with are **not one node**: one is a figure, one is an animal in a den, and this edge says they share a word without saying they share anything else.
That separation is the whole reason the type exists. Merging them would make the graph assert that a symbol and a beast are the same entity, and a reader following the edge would arrive at Revelation from Daniel with nothing marking the crossing. Kept apart and linked, a search on *lion* returns Daniel's den, David's kill, Samson's riddle, Judah's lion and Peter's, in one list, with none of them claiming to be another.
Not every image has a tangible counterpart -- shadow, vapour and chaff are words the corpus only ever uses figuratively -- and those images simply carry no `drawn_from` edge.

likened_to.label: is likened to
likened_to.inverse: is used as an image for
likened_to.notes: A comparison the text marks -- "like a roaring lion" (1Pet 5:8), "like chaff driven off by the wind" (Ps 1:4). The tenor is the source and the image the target: "the devil is likened to a lion", never the reverse (a dozen edges ran image-first until 2026-10-02, so cards read "lightning is likened to Jesus"). The note carries the *ground*, the respect in which, wherever the verse states it: Revelation's lion has prevailed and Peter's walks about seeking whom he may devour, and with the ground recorded they are visibly two figures sharing a noun.

made.label: made
made.notes: Bezalel and the ark (Exod 37:1), Moses and the bronze snake (Num 21:9). Who fashioned the thing, where the text says so; commissioning is `commanded_the_making_of`, because Exodus keeps them apart.

commanded_the_making_of.label: commanded the making of
commanded_the_making_of.notes: Distinct from `made`. Exodus is careful about it: the pattern is shown to Moses on the mountain (Exod 25:9, 40) and Bezalel does the work (Exod 37:1). Collapsing the two would credit the wrong hand.

wore.label: wore
wore.notes:
Clothing the text puts on a named person. Aaron and the ephod, the breastpiece of judgment and the turban (Exod 28); David wearing a linen ephod (2Sam 6:14); Joshua the high priest and the clean turban (Zech 3:5).
`carried` was the nearest existing type and it is not the same claim. Abiathar carrying the ephod to David so he can enquire (1Sam 23:9) is a different act from Aaron wearing it into the holy place, and collapsing the two would lose the distinction the priesthood chapters are built on -- the garments are worn *to bear the names of the tribes* into the presence, not transported.
Says nothing about who was entitled to wear a thing. Gideon's ephod and Aaron's are both worn and the corpus judges them very differently; that judgement is in the verses, not in this edge.

kept_at.label: was kept at
kept_at.notes: The ark at Kirjath-jearim (1Sam 7:1), in the house of Obed-edom (2Sam 6:11). Objects move, so this is expected to be many-valued and each resting place carries its own citation.

worshiped.label: worshiped
worshiped.notes: The text's own verb and nothing more: "they worshiped other gods" (Judg 2:17), the golden calf (Exod 32:8). Approved by Doug 2026-11-08 (P-2026-11-07-3): other gods' 76 verses all state service or worship, and none could be recorded. Who is worshiped rightly is never this edge's to say.

served.label: served
served.notes: Service as the text means it of gods and idols: "they forsook the LORD and served the Baals" (Judg 2:13). Not a servant's work for a master (servant_of). Approved by Doug 2026-11-08 (P-2026-11-07-3).

kind_of.label: is one of the
kind_of.notes: A particular thing the text follows, linked to the card of its kind (plan A.45, approved 2026-11-06: "a common kind with its instances (oxen, wells), each instance its own card, linked as the same kind, never the same one"). The twelve stones from the Jordan are one of the stones; they are not the stones of Stephen's stoning. Added 2026-11-08 with the first A.45 nodes.

signifies.label: signifies
signifies.group: What the text says it stands for
signifies.notes:
**The text's own key, and only ever that.** "That Rock was Christ" (1Cor 10:4), "the field is the world" (Matt 13:38), "the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches" (Rev 1:20). The graph is not deciding that a rock means Christ; it is recording that Paul wrote it, with the verse he wrote it in.
This is the one place the graph holds a meaning rather than a comparison, which is why it is restricted to identifications the corpus states outright. `likened_to` is the weaker neighbour and holds "is like", leaving the meaning alone; `draws_on` is weaker still and holds only that a title is built on a word. Where the text merely juxtaposes two things, none of the three applies and nothing is recorded.
A key is not transitive and must not be walked as though it were. Paul reads the rock at Horeb as Christ; that says nothing about every other rock in the corpus, and the physical rock keeps its own verses and its own place in Exodus 17 either way.

answered_in.label: is answered in
answered_in.notes: **Position, not identity.** The story's part and the explanation's part stand in the same place, and the citation is the explanation's verse. A card shows the mark by its `answer_kind` and never as an equals sign. Where the text itself says "the seed is ..." the relation is `signifies`, not this.

bought.label: bought
bought.notes:
A purchase the text records with a price and usually a named seller. 60 verses use bought or purchase, and the land transactions among them are foundational rather than incidental: Abraham buying Machpelah of Ephron (Gen 23:16-17), the first ground he owned in Canaan and the tomb of four generations; David buying the threshingfloor of Araunah rather than take it free, "I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing" (2Sam 24:24); Omri buying the hill Samaria of Shemer and naming the city after the man he bought it from (1Kgs 16:24); Jacob at Shechem (Gen 33:19), where Joseph was later buried (Josh 24:32); Jeremiah buying a field in Anathoth while the Babylonians besieged the city (Jer 32:9).
The seller is named in the note rather than given an edge of its own. A purchase is one act, and recording it twice from both ends would double every transaction to say nothing new.

built.label: built
built.notes: Cain and the city of Enoch (Gen 4:17), Solomon and the house of the LORD (1Kgs 6:14), the sons of Hassenaah and the fish gate (Neh 3:3). Who raised the structure, where the text says so. `made` is the equivalent for objects, and the two are kept apart because a gate stays where it is put and an ark does not.

repaired.label: repaired
repaired.notes: Kept separate from `built` because Nehemiah 3 says both, thirty-five times each, and a reader who is told Hanun "built" the valley gate when the verse says "repaired" has been told something the text did not say. Where a verse says both of the same party and the same gate -- "the valley gate repaired Hanun ... they built it" (Neh 3:13) -- both are recorded, rather than one being chosen on the graph's behalf.

ruler_of.label: was ruler of
ruler_of.notes: The district officer, not the king: "Rephaiah son of Hur, ruler of a half-district of Jerusalem" (Neh 3:9). Nehemiah 3 names nine of them and halves several districts between two men, which `reigned_over` cannot express and should not be asked to -- it is reserved for a throne over a realm.

instituted.label: instituted
instituted.notes: Where the text names who established the practice. Much of the law is given without a human institutor, and that absence is left as it stands rather than filled in.

observed.label: kept
observed.notes: A named keeping: Josiah's passover (2Kgs 23:22), Hezekiah's (2Chr 30:1). Not every mention -- the point is an occasion the text records.

father_of.label: is the father of
father_of.notes: Biological or legally-recognized father. In Hebrew idiom "son of" can mean any male ancestor (Matt 1:1, "Jesus Christ, the son of David"); use ancestor_of for those. Use this only where a direct generation is meant.

sibling_of.label: is a sibling of
sibling_of.notes: Full or unspecified siblings. Use half_sibling_of when the text is explicit about a shared single parent (e.g. Amnon and Tamar, 2Sam 13:1-4).

ancestor_of.label: is an ancestor of
ancestor_of.notes: Multi-generation descent, or descent asserted without the intervening generations being given. Genealogy chains (Matt 1, Luke 3, 1Chr 1-9) produce father_of edges link-by-link; use ancestor_of for the summary claims the text makes directly ("son of David, son of Abraham"), and for a people descended from a named ancestor (Gen 10, Gen 25:3).

uncle_of.label: is the uncle/aunt of
uncle_of.notes: Recorded where the text states it: "Saul's uncle Ner" (1Sam 14:50), "his mother's brother Laban" (Gen 29:10). Where both the parent and the sibling are named, record those instead and let the relationship follow from them. Not Mark and Barnabas: Col 4:10's ἀνεψιός is a cousin, and the KJV's "sister's son" put an uncle edge in the graph that the Greek does not support (moved to `cousin_of`, 2026-10-02).

cousin_of.label: is the cousin of
cousin_of.notes: Only where the text itself says cousin: "Mark the cousin of Barnabas" (Col 4:10, Greek ἀνεψιός). Normally a cousin is inferred from two parents who are siblings, and then it is not recorded here -- record the parents and the siblings and let it follow from them.

adoptive_parent_of.label: raised / adopted
adoptive_parent_of.notes: Mordecai and Esther (Esth 2:7); Pharaoh's daughter and Moses (Exod 2:10).

concubine_of.label: is a concubine of
concubine_of.notes: Source is the concubine, target is the man. Recorded because the text distinguishes the status and it affects succession claims (2Sam 3:7).

predecessor_of.label: was succeeded by
predecessor_of.notes: Source held an office (king, high priest, judge, governor) and target held it next. Direction is always earlier -> later.

appointed.label: appointed / installed
appointed.notes:
Placing someone in an office or command (1Kgs 4:1-6; Acts 6:3-6).
A body as often as a man at either end. David sets the Levites over the service of song (1Chr 6:31) and divides them into courses (1Chr 23:6); the Levites in turn appoint the singers (1Chr 15:17). An office conferred on a standing body is the same act as one conferred on a person, and refusing it would drop the arrangement Chronicles spends whole chapters describing.

offered.label: offered
offered.notes:
The text's own verb, and it is deliberately the only thing this records. Genesis 22:2 has "Offer him there as a burnt offering", Hebrews 11:17 "By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac", James 2:21 "justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar" -- three books, one word, and none of them says the offering was completed.
So this type carries the act and not its outcome. Whether the thing offered died is a separate fact with its own citation: at Moriah the angel stops him (Gen 22:12) and a ram is offered "in place of his son" (22:13), and both are recorded as their own edges.

speaks_of.label: speaks of
speaks_of.notes:
Joins a cited statement to the word it makes a claim about. "God is love" (1John 4:8) speaks of love; "now these three remain: faith, hope, and love" (1Cor 13:13) speaks of all three.
**The direction matters and is the whole discipline of the type.** The statement is the thing with a verse behind it; the concept is a place for statements to gather. Nothing runs the other way, because a concept has nothing of its own to say -- there is no edge from `love` asserting what love is, and there should not be one.
That also settles how concepts relate to each other: **they do not, directly.** Faith, hope and charity are joined because one verse names all three and speaks of each, so the path between them runs through the text that makes the claim and a reader following it arrives at the evidence. An edge straight from faith to hope would assert a relation the corpus states nowhere.
Not a route in from people. "Abraham believed God" is a verse about Abraham, and pointing it at `faith` would turn the type into an attribute system -- who had what virtue -- which is a different design and one this project has not made. Where the corpus commends a person for something, `draws_on` already runs from the text to the person, and the concept is reached through the same text.

came_upon.label: came upon
came_upon.inverse: had the Spirit come upon them
came_upon.notes:
**The corpus's most characteristic statement about the Spirit, and until this type existed the graph could not hold a single instance of it.** Forty-one verses say the Spirit came upon, came mightily upon, rested upon, fell upon, moved, or filled a named person or company, from Judges to Acts, and none of them fit any existing type. The Spirit was in the graph with nineteen edges, every one of them either an image or another member of the deity, and none of them an act on a human being.
One phrase and one claim: **the verse says the Spirit came upon this person.** What followed is in the citation and not in the edge. Othniel judged, Gideon blew a trumpet, Samson tore a lion, Saul prophesied, Bezaleel made the tabernacle furniture, Peter answered the council, Stephen looked up -- and the type asserts none of it, because the corpus is not consistent about what the coming produces and a type that named a consequence would have to pick one.
Deliberately not in the `deity` category, which is scoped to what the corpus says about the Father, the Son and the Spirit **in relation to one another**. This is the Spirit and a person, and it belongs beside `anointed`, which the corpus twice puts in the same sentence: "Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him ... and the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward" (1Sam 16:13).
**The type says nothing about permanence and the corpus does not either.** One verse after David, Saul loses it -- "the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul" (1Sam 16:14) -- and Saul's own edge from 1 Samuel 10 remains true of the chapter that states it. Where the corpus records a departure the note carries it; there is no separate type for it, and inventing one would put a two-instance edge in the vocabulary to hold what a citation already holds.

anointed.label: anointed
anointed.notes:
Samuel anointed Saul (1Sam 10:1) and David (1Sam 16:13).
A body of people as often as a prophet, and the difference is not incidental: "the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah" (2Sam 2:4), "all the elders of Israel ... anointed David king over Israel" (1Chr 11:3), "the people of the land took Jehoahaz ... and anointed him" (2Kgs 23:30). Refusing a group here would record who held the horn and lose who conferred the office.

servant_of.label: served
servant_of.notes:
Source serves target. Covers officials, armour-bearers, stewards and slaves alike; the text rarely separates them cleanly.
A being is allowed as target because "my servant" is a title the corpus gives repeatedly and in God's own voice -- "my servant Abraham" (Gen 26:24), "my servant Moses" (Num 12:7), "my servant David" (2Sam 3:18), "my servant Job" (Job 1:8). Refusing it would drop a formula the text states outright.

commander_of.label: commanded the army of
commander_of.notes: Joab under David (2Sam 8:16); Abner under Saul (1Sam 14:50).

counselor_of.label: was counselor to
counselor_of.notes: Ahithophel to David and then Absalom (2Sam 15:12; 16:23).

prophet_to.label: prophesied to / confronted
prophet_to.notes: Nathan to David (2Sam 12:1-7); Elijah to Ahab (1Kgs 18:17-18).

mentor_of.label: was mentor / master to
mentor_of.notes: Elijah and Elisha (1Kgs 19:19-21); Paul and Timothy (1Tim 1:2).

blessed.label: blessed
blessed.notes:
Formal, consequential blessings (Gen 27:27-29), not casual greetings.
A being is allowed as source because most of the blessings in the corpus are God's, and a type that could only carry Isaac blessing Jacob would record the derivative case and refuse the original.

healed.label: healed / raised
healed.notes: Physical healing, exorcism, or raising from the dead, where the text names or clearly identifies the person. Unnamed but individuated people count ("the woman with the issue of blood", "the centurion's servant") — give them a descriptive id and say so in the disambiguation.

ministered_to.label: taught / ministered to
ministered_to.notes: A substantial personal encounter that is neither healing nor formal discipleship: the woman at the well (John 4:7-26), Nicodemus (John 3:1-10), Zacchaeus (Luke 19:5-9), the rich young ruler. Use mentor_of for an ongoing master-disciple bond, and healed when the outcome is a cure.

ally_of.label: was allied with
ally_of.notes: Political or military alliance (1Kgs 22:4), not mere friendship.

companion_of.label: traveled / worked with
companion_of.notes: Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:2); missionary and ministry partners.

persecuted.label: persecuted / sought to kill
persecuted.notes: The word for Saul toward David: sustained pursuit of harm by someone with power over the target (1Sam 19:1-2, 23:14). For a single act of violence use killed or attacked; for scheming use conspired_against.

enemy_of.label: was an enemy of
enemy_of.notes: Declared or sustained hostility where neither side is clearly the aggressor.

contrary_to.label: is contrary to
contrary_to.group: What the text sets against it
contrary_to.notes:
The corpus sets two things against each other. "The flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other" (Gal 5:17). "What fellowship does light have with darkness?" (2Cor 6:14). "God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all" (1John 1:5).
**The opposition must be the text's, not the reader's.** This is the easiest type in the vocabulary to overuse, because almost any two things can be made to look opposed by someone who wants them to be, and an edge that says "contrary" carries more weight than most. Use it where the corpus states the contrast -- says they are contrary, asks what one has to do with the other, denies that one is in the other at all -- or where it builds the contrast structurally, as the regnal formulas do by giving every reign one verdict or the other and never both.
**Do not use it for tensions the corpus leaves standing.** Rom 4:3 and Jas 2:24 are held apart by readers, not by the text. Marking them contrary would settle by vocabulary what the corpus declines to settle, and this graph's whole claim is that it does not do that.
Nor is it for people who opposed each other -- that is `enemy_of`, or `rebuked`, or `conspired_against`. Paul withstood Peter to the face without either becoming the other's opposite.

conspired_against.label: conspired against
conspired_against.inverse: was the target of a conspiracy by

betrayed.label: betrayed
betrayed.notes:
Judas and Jesus (Matt 26:14-16, 48-49).
A body of people as often as one man, on the same reasoning as prophet_to: the Ziphites carry David's hiding place to Saul twice (1Sam 23:19, 26:1), and the men of Keilah would have delivered him up had he stayed (1Sam 23:12).

killed.label: killed
killed.notes: Direct responsibility, including ordering the death (2Sam 12:9, where the text charges David with Uriah's death). Note the ordering in the relation's note when it is indirect.

deceived.label: deceived
deceived.notes: Jacob and Isaac (Gen 27:19); Gibeonites and Joshua (Josh 9:3-15); the serpent and Eve (Gen 3:13).

cast_into.label: was cast into
cast_into.notes:
Someone put somewhere against their will and kept there: Daniel into the den of lions (Dan 6:16), the three into the burning fiery furnace (Dan 3:21), Joseph into the pit (Gen 37:24), Jeremiah into the dungeon (Jer 38:6), Jonah into the sea (Jonah 1:15).
The source is the one who ends up inside, not the one doing the throwing, because that is the fact the reader is looking for and the thrower is usually a crowd the text does not name. Who ordered it is recorded separately where the corpus says -- Nebuchadnezzar commands the furnace heated and Darius signs the decree he then cannot undo.
`imprisoned` joins two people and is the right type for a captivity. This one joins a person to the thing, because in these episodes the thing is the point: the furnace is heated seven times more than it was wont, and the stone on the den is sealed with the king's own signet.

founded.label: founded
founded.notes: For the Chronicles idiom "X the father of Y" where Y is a town -- "Ashhur the father of Tekoa" (1Chr 2:24, 4:5), "Penuel was the father of Gedor" (1Chr 4:4), "Hur ... the father of Bethlehem" (1Chr 4:4). The standard reading is founder, or principal ancestor of the town's inhabitants; the vocabulary translates the idiom the way it translates "fathered" as father_of. **Always quote the phrase in the relation's note**, so a reader sees the words the text used and can weigh the reading. Not mechanically separable from genuine paternity: "Hamor the father of Shechem" (Gen 34:6) is a real father and son who also names a city. Decide per instance, and use father_of where the son is a person.

born_at.label: was born at
born_at.notes: Jesus at Bethlehem (Luke 2:4-7); use only where the text says born, not merely present.

buried_at.label: was buried at
buried_at.notes: Sarah in the cave of Machpelah (Gen 23:19); Jacob's burial (Gen 50:13).

dwelt_at.label: lived at
dwelt_at.notes: A settled residence the text establishes, not a single visit. Abraham at Hebron (Gen 13:18); Paul at Corinth for a year and six months (Acts 18:11).

stationed_at.label: was stationed at
stationed_at.notes:
Where the text posts a being or a creature and leaves it there. The cherubim at the east of Eden with the flaming sword (Gen 3:24); the two over the mercy seat, from between which God says he will speak (Exod 25:20-22); the cherubim Ezekiel sees at the threshold of the house (Ezek 10:18-19).
`dwelt_at` will not carry these, and the reason is worth stating: it takes a person or a group, because a settled human residence is what it was built for. A cherub is neither, and forcing it into `dwelt_at` would claim the cherubim *lived* in Eden -- which is a reading of Genesis 3:24, not what it says. The text says they were placed.
Placement, not residence, and not purpose. Genesis says the cherubim were put there "to keep the way of the tree of life"; that clause is in the citation where a reader can weigh it, and this type does not restate it as a claim about what cherubim are for.

reigned_over.label: reigned over
reigned_over.notes: The realm, not the seat. "Ahab began to reign over Israel" (1Kgs 16:29) and "Ahab ruled from Samaria" are two different facts, and the text states them separately -- often in the same verse. Without this the reigns had nowhere to go: they were recorded as `led` against the people, which is what a judge does, and left the kingdoms themselves nearly unconnected. Distinct from `led`, which the text reserves for judging and for leading men into battle.

ruled_from.label: ruled from
ruled_from.notes: David reigning from Hebron then Jerusalem (2Sam 5:5).

traveled_to.label: went to
traveled_to.notes: A journey the narrative marks. Deliberately weak: nearly everyone goes nearly everywhere, and recording each move would swamp the stronger ties.

member_of.label: belonged to
member_of.notes: Only where the text places the person in the group: Saul a Benjamite (1Sam 9:1), Paul a Pharisee (Acts 23:6), Barnabas a Levite (Acts 4:36).

led.label: led
led.notes: Moses and Israel, Joab and David's army, a judge over the people -- and the LORD leading one person, which is most of the Psalms and Prophets.

present_with.label: is with
present_with.notes: Only where the text states the presence. Omnipresence is a doctrine and not a citation; this type records verses that say someone is with someone.

descended_from_person.label: descends from
descended_from_person.notes: A tribe or nation to the person it is named for and traced from: the children of Judah from Judah, the Moabites from Moab (Gen 19:37). This is how the text itself explains a people's origin, and it is what keeps the person Moab and the nation Moab distinct while joined.

fought.label: made war on
fought.notes: Either side may be a person or a people, because the text puts it both ways: "Saul struck down the Amalekites" (1Sam 15:7) and "So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated" (1Sam 4:10), which names no commander at all. Use attacked for violence between two named individuals.

conquered.label: conquered
conquered.notes: Subjugation with a lasting outcome, distinct from a battle: Assyria carrying Israel away (2Kgs 17:6), Babylon taking Judah (2Kgs 25:21). The exile is one of the central facts of the Old Testament and names no single actor on the losing side, which is why this takes groups at both ends. Record the battle as fought and the outcome as conquered where the text gives both.

wrote_to.label: wrote to
wrote_to.notes: An epistle addressed to a congregation, cited from the salutation that names it: "To the saints in Ephesus" (Eph 1:1), "To the church of God in Corinth" (1Cor 1:2). The target is the CHURCH, which is a group, not the town it met in — Paul wrote to people, and the place is a fact about them rather than the addressee. Join the church to its town with based_at. Record only what the letter's own address gives, not where tradition says it was written or sent. Where a letter names no addressee — Hebrews, James, 1 John — there is nothing to record.

wrote_letter_to.label: wrote to
wrote_letter_to.notes: The counterpart for letters addressed to a person rather than a congregation: Paul to Timothy, Titus and Philemon, John to Gaius (3John 1).

based_at.label: centered on
based_at.notes: Joins a congregation, household or tribe to the place it belongs to, so that "the church at Ephesus" is a group with a location rather than a synonym for the town.

located_in.label: is in
located_in.notes: Place to place — Bethlehem in Judah, Capernaum in Galilee.

judged.label: passed judgment on
judged.notes: Pilate and Jesus (John 19:13-16); formal legal proceedings.

aspect_of.label: is an aspect of
aspect_of.notes: "God as Creator" is an aspect of God; "Spirit in Creation" of the Holy Spirit; "Sacrifice as Worship" of sacrifice. Each aspect is its own node because scripture describes it on its own (the passages it cites), and it is joined to the idea it is a facet of rather than merged into it.

in_theme.label: is a core concept of the major theme
in_theme.notes: "Covenant Signs" is a core concept of the major theme Covenant; "the day of atonement" (an observance) of the major theme Sacrifice. The theme's own page lists its concepts with their passages.

quotes.label: quotes
quotes.notes: The Berean editors' note that this verse quotes that one. Stated by the editors; the words in common are on the verse page.

points_to.label: points to
points_to.notes: The Berean editors refer this verse, or the section it opens, to that one: a note, or the list of passages under a section heading (which for the gospels is the parallel accounts, and elsewhere is not: Isaiah 53's lists 1 Peter 2:21). Stated by the editors; what the two share is not said.

says_the_same_as.label: says the same as
says_the_same_as.notes: A pair the alignment found and a model judged to say the same thing: a parallel account, one promise said twice, or a prophecy and its quotation. Always a reading. The editors' section lists are points_to.

alludes_to.label: alludes to
alludes_to.notes: This verse takes up words or an image of that one without quoting it, as judged by a reader of both. Always a reading.

echoes.label: echoes
echoes.notes: A later verse shares rare words with an earlier one, found by matching the original languages, not by reading. Each carries its grade: "strong" is about 5 in 8 real, "likely" about 4 in 8. Not a claim that the later verse quotes or means the earlier.

spoke_to.definition: That one spoke to another, as the narrator tells it: "Isaac said to Abraham" (Gen 22:7). The speech turn is its evidence; what was said is the turn's content, not this relation.
spoke_to.by: drafted by Claude Opus, 2026-10-20, from the approved recommendation (G1, the 1.2.0 inventory)

states.definition: A statement one clause of the text makes, its subject doing to its object what the verb says: "God loved the world" (John 3:16). The verb is carried with the claim as the verse renders it, with its grammar, the force it is said with and the kind of act it names. Only a statement made outright, by a verb whose form says it happened, is asserted; a command, promise, prediction or purpose is described and never stated. The plain triple carries no verb (every statement uses this one type): read the claim, whose claim:verb and claim:modality say what was said and how.
states.by: drafted by Claude Opus, 2026-10-19, for Doug's review with the 1.2.0 inventory

deity_of.definition: A divine being is called the God of a person or people, as in the text's formula "the God of" a patriarch or of Israel; it is a relationship the text states and not an identification of the two.
deity_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

self_designated_as.definition: A person or being applies a title to himself in his own speech, as against a title that the narrator or another speaker gives him; it records who said the words and not what follows from them.
self_designated_as.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

spoken_of_as.definition: The text applies the name or nature of one person or being to another; the edge says only that a particular verse says so, and it is not a claim that the two are the same.
spoken_of_as.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

quoted.definition: A speaker or writing takes up the words of another speaker or writing; the target is the person the text credits with the words, not the book they are found in.
quoted.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

named_with.definition: The text names the two together in a single formula or sentence; the edge records the joint naming and does not say how the two are related.
named_with.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

distinguished_from.definition: The text sets the two apart, for example when a speaker contrasts himself with another; it records the statement and does not settle what the contrast means.
distinguished_from.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

put_away.definition: A person or group sends another away to end a marriage, in the text's own word and not in a later legal term such as divorce.
put_away.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

accused.definition: A person or group lays a charge against another person or group; it is the complaint made, not a plot against someone and not the verdict.
accused.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

charged.definition: A person, being or group lays a binding instruction on another, stronger than a request.
charged.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

besought.definition: A person or group entreats another where the text marks the act as a petition; the polite "please" of ordinary speech is not recorded.
besought.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

rebuked.definition: A person, being or group reproves another in an episode the narrative reports; a letter that itself delivers a reproof, without reporting a confrontation, does not make an edge to its readers.
rebuked.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

warned.definition: A person, being or group gives another notice of danger or of a consequence to come.
warned.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

told.definition: A person, being or group gives a parable, dream or vision, the one the figure belongs to; it is not the one who wrote it down.
told.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

explained.definition: A person, being or group gives the interpretation of a parable, dream or vision; it is kept apart from telling because the two are often different people.
explained.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

sent.definition: A person, being or group sends another person, being, group or creature, where the text narrates the sending.
sent.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

assumed_form_of.definition: A temporary form is the form that a person or being took on and later set aside, where the text narrates the taking; the form is the source and the one who took it is the target.
assumed_form_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

appeared_to.definition: A being, person or group appears to a person or group in a visitation the text narrates, without classifying it as a vision, a dream or a bodily appearance.
appeared_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

party_to.definition: A person, group or being is named by the text as a party to a covenant.
party_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

token_of.definition: An object, observance, creature or place is named by the text as the sign of a covenant.
token_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

supersedes.definition: One covenant is said by the text to make an earlier covenant obsolete; it is recorded only where the text says so.
supersedes.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

assessed_as.definition: A subject is the doer of a deed that the text itself evaluates, such as the verdict pronounced on a reign or on a part of creation; the evaluation is the text's own and not a reader's.
assessed_as.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

described_as.definition: A subject is said by the text to be a certain way: an age, a state, a trait, a role or a verdict on the subject itself, as distinct from a deed that is evaluated.
described_as.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

titled.definition: A person or being is called by a title that the text gives; the title is its own entity, kept apart from the creature or object it is built from.
titled.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

asserted_by.definition: A claim, verdict, title or saying is vouched for by a named party, or by the writing itself where no speaker is named; it lets two differing claims be held side by side without being joined.
asserted_by.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

grounds.definition: One statement is the reason the text gives for another, so that the second rests on the first.
grounds.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

conditional_on.definition: A consequence the text states is tied to the condition on which it depends, as in a bargain, a blessing or a warning that begins "if".
conditional_on.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

recounts.definition: A telling is one account of an event or of another telling, so that two writings can describe the same thing without being merged into one voice.
recounts.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

incited.definition: One party moves another to act, in the sense of causing someone to take an action; the action itself is carried by what the one moved then does.
incited.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

gave.definition: A person, being or group transfers something to another; the edge records the giving and not what the gift came to mean.
gave.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

took.definition: A person, being or group takes something from another or from its place; the counterpart of giving.
took.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

ate.definition: A person, being, group or creature eats something, where the text records the eating.
ate.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

heard.definition: A person, being or group hears a speech, a cry or a report, where the text records the hearing.
heard.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

answered.definition: One speech replies to another, or a person replies to a speech or a person; where the text has a speaker answer the previous speech, the reply is to what was said and not only to the one who said it.
answered.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

named.definition: A person, being or group gives a name to someone or something, or changes an existing name, where the text says who did the naming.
named.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

destroyed.definition: A person, being or group destroys a place, people, thing or creature, where the text says so.
destroyed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

issues_from.definition: One thing comes out of another as its source; it is origin and not containment, and a river that goes out of a place is not a part of it.
issues_from.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

ascribed_to.definition: A writing carries a superscription naming a person or group; the edge records the ascription as it is printed and does not say whether it means authorship, dedication or subject.
ascribed_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

part_of.definition: One unit of the text lies inside a larger unit, such as a saying within a psalm or a passage within a longer passage; the relation is containment and is passed on through each level.
part_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

spoken_in.definition: A kind of message is spoken within a pattern, concept, event or passage; it is supported by the verses the message and the other node share, and not by the names sounding alike.
spoken_in.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

specializes.definition: One form is a narrower form of a broader form; both are forms and neither is an occurrence, and the grouping is the graph's own and not a statement of the text.
specializes.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

instance_of.definition: A passage, saying, event or group is one case of a shape that several passages share; the shape is the graph's grouping and not a claim that the writers intended one.
instance_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

re_enacts.definition: A later account is told so as to re-enact an earlier one; the grade of the edge says whether the text states it, a quotation carries it, or a reader's correspondence alone supports it.
re_enacts.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

takes_up.definition: A later account quotes, summarises or gathers the words given in an earlier one; the pairs of words are the evidence and no likeness between persons is claimed.
takes_up.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

same_steps_as.definition: Two accounts have the same sequence of steps, each step quoted from both texts; the edge makes no claim that either was told with the other in mind.
same_steps_as.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

possibly_same_as.definition: Two person records that the text never joins may, in a reader's view, be one person; this is not an identity, each record keeps its own verses, and the evidence is given on both sides.
possibly_same_as.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

occasion_of.definition: An event is an occasion of a significant number, being a time the text counts as that span; the edge is cited to the verse that counts it and claims no meaning for the number.
occasion_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

composed_of.definition: A phrase is built from the words of a term; this is a fact about the wording only and does not say that the phrase is a kind of that thing.
composed_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

draws_on.definition: A title, saying or image is built on another image, person, place, being or text; this is a claim about wording and not about what the image means.
draws_on.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

drawn_from.definition: A word used as an image is joined to the tangible thing of the same name, where the graph holds one; the two share a word and are not one node.
drawn_from.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

likened_to.definition: The text marks a comparison in which the first is compared to the second, the thing described being the source and the image the target.
likened_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

made.definition: A person, group or being fashions or creates something, where the text names the maker; commissioning the work is a separate relation.
made.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

commanded_the_making_of.definition: A person or being commands that something be made, which is kept apart from the one who does the making.
commanded_the_making_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

wore.definition: A person or group wears a garment or piece of dress the text puts on them; it is not the same as carrying the garment and says nothing of who had the right to wear it.
wore.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

kept_at.definition: An object, concept or creature is kept at a place; an object that moves can have several such places, each with its own citation.
kept_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

carried.definition: A person or group bears or transports an object, concept or creature.
carried.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

signifies.definition: The text states outright what a thing stands for; it records the key the text gives and not a reader's decision about what something means, and it does not carry over to other uses of the same word.
signifies.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

answered_in.definition: A part of a story is taken up in a part of its explanation, in the same place in the telling; it records where the text's explanation answers the story and not that the two are the same thing, which is what signifies records when the text says so outright.
answered_in.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, in the parable mapping Doug Egge ruled on 2026-10-29

bought.definition: A person or group buys a place, object or thing, in a purchase the text records.
bought.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

built.definition: A person, group or being raises a place or structure, where the text says who built it.
built.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

repaired.definition: A person or group repairs a place or structure; it is kept apart from building because the text distinguishes the two.
repaired.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

ruler_of.definition: A person holds a district office over a place or group; it is a ruling office and not a throne, and one district may have more than one such officer.
ruler_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

instituted.definition: A person or being establishes an observance, where the text names who established it.
instituted.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

observed.definition: A person or group keeps an observance on an occasion the text records.

half_sibling_of.definition: Two people share one parent, where the text is explicit about it; the relation reads the same from either side.

ancestor_of.definition: A person or group is an ancestor of another across more than one generation, or without the intervening generations being given, including a people traced to a named ancestor.

uncle_of.definition: A person is the uncle or aunt of another, recorded where the text states it and not where it follows from two named parents and a sibling.

cousin_of.definition: Two people are cousins, recorded only where the text itself says so; the relation reads the same from either side.
cousin_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

adoptive_parent_of.definition: A person who becomes a parent of another through a willful, formal process of adoption.

spouse_of.definition: Two people are married to each other; the relation reads the same from either side.
spouse_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

concubine_of.definition: A woman is a concubine of a man, a status the text distinguishes from marriage; the concubine is the source and the man the target.
concubine_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

betrothed_to.definition: Two people are betrothed to each other before marriage; the relation reads the same from either side.
betrothed_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

predecessor_of.definition: A person held an office, such as king, high priest or judge, and another held it next; the direction always runs from the earlier holder to the later.
predecessor_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

co_regent_with.definition: Two people reigned jointly; the relation reads the same from either side.
co_regent_with.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

appointed.definition: A person, group or being places a person or group in an office or command.
appointed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

offered.definition: A person or group offers a person, creature or object as a sacrifice; it records the act the text names and not whether the offering was carried through.
offered.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

speaks_of.definition: A statement, title, image or verdict makes a claim about the thing it names; the statement is the source with the verse behind it, and nothing runs the other way.
speaks_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

came_upon.definition: The Spirit or another being comes upon a person or group, as the text puts it; the edge says the verse reports this and does not say what the coming produced or how long it lasted.
came_upon.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

anointed.definition: A person or group anoints a person, as the text records it; a body of people can confer the office as well as a prophet.
anointed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

deposed.definition: A person is removed from power by another.
deposed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

servant_of.definition: A person, group or concept serves a person, group or being; the relation covers officials, armour-bearers, stewards and slaves alike, since the text rarely separates them.
servant_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

commander_of.definition: A person commanded the army of another.
commander_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

counselor_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

prophet_to.definition: A person speaks as a prophet to a person or group, confronting them with a message.
prophet_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

mentor_of.definition: A person was the master or mentor of another, who was the disciple.
mentor_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

blessed.definition: A being, person or group pronounces a formal and consequential blessing on a person or group, not a casual greeting.
blessed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

cursed.definition: A person or being pronounces a curse on a person, group, place, creature, object or being.
cursed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

baptized.definition: A person or being baptizes a person or group.
baptized.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

healed.definition: A person or being heals, casts out a spirit from, or raises from the dead, a person or group the text names or clearly picks out.
healed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

ministered_to.definition: A person, group or being teaches or ministers to another in a substantial personal encounter that is neither a healing nor an ongoing discipleship.
ministered_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

ally_of.definition: Two parties were allied politically or militarily; the relation reads the same from either side and is not a mere friendship.
ally_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

friend_of.definition: Two people were close friends; the relation reads the same from either side.
friend_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

companion_of.definition: Two people travelled or worked together; the relation reads the same from either side.
companion_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

persecuted.definition: A person or group pursued another with sustained harm, from a position of power over them, and not by a single act of violence.
persecuted.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

enemy_of.definition: Two parties were declared or lasting enemies where neither is clearly the aggressor; the relation reads the same from either side.
enemy_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

contrary_to.definition: The text sets two things against each other, by saying they are contrary or by building the contrast into its structure; the opposition is the text's and not a reader's, and tensions the text leaves standing are not recorded.
contrary_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

conspired_against.definition: A person, group or being plots against a person or group.
conspired_against.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

betrayed.definition: A person or group betrays another person or group.
betrayed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

kind_of.definition: A particular object or creature the text follows is one of a kind: the twelve stones from the Jordan are one of the stones, never the same as another instance of that kind.
kind_of.by: drafted by Claude Opus under plan A.45 (approved by Doug Egge, 2026-11-06)

killed.definition: A person, group or being kills a person, group or creature, including by ordering the death.
killed.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

attacked.definition: A person, group or being attacks or makes war on a person or group.
attacked.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

deceived.definition: A person, group, being or creature deceives a person, group or being.
deceived.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

cast_into.definition: A person or group is put into a place or object against their will and kept there; the source is the one who ends up inside and not the one who threw them.

imprisoned.definition: A person or group holds another person, group or concept in captivity.
imprisoned.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

born_at.definition: A person was born at a place, recorded only where the text says born and not merely present.
born_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

died_at.definition: A person died at a place.
died_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

buried_at.definition: A person was buried at a place or object.
buried_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

dwelt_at.definition: A person or group lived at a place, a settled residence the text establishes and not a single visit.
dwelt_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

stationed_at.definition: A being or creature is posted at a place or object and left there; it records the placement and not residence or purpose.
stationed_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

reigned_over.definition: A person reigned over a realm or a people; the realm and the seat of government are separate facts.
reigned_over.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

ruled_from.definition: A person ruled from a place that was the seat of the rule.
ruled_from.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

traveled_to.definition: A person or group went to a place on a journey the narrative marks; it is deliberately a weak tie.
traveled_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

member_of.definition: A person or concept belonged to a group, recorded only where the text places them in it.
member_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

led.definition: A person, being, group or concept leads a person or group, including the leading of one person by God.
led.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

present_with.definition: A being, person, group or concept is with a person, group, being or concept, where the text states the presence in so many words.
present_with.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

descended_from_person.definition: A tribe or nation descends from the person it is named for, as the text explains the origin of a people; the person and the people remain separate nodes.
descended_from_person.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

fought.definition: A person or group made war on a person or group, where either side may be a person or a people.
fought.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

conquered.definition: A person or group subjugated another with a lasting outcome, as distinct from a single battle.
conquered.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

wrote_to.definition: A person wrote to a congregation, taken from the address of the letter itself; the target is the group and not the town where it met.
wrote_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

worshiped.definition: A person or group worships a god, an idol or another object of worship, as the text says of them.
worshiped.by: drafted by Claude Opus, approved by Doug Egge (P-2026-11-07-3, 2026-11-08)

wrote_letter_to.definition: A person wrote to another person, taken from the address of the letter itself.
wrote_letter_to.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

based_at.definition: A group is centered on a place, so that a church, household or tribe is a group with a location and not a synonym for the place.
based_at.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

located_in.definition: A place or object lies within a larger place.
located_in.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

judged.definition: A person, group or being passes judgment on a person or group, in a formal legal proceeding or a pronounced verdict.
judged.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

aspect_of.definition: A concept or pattern is one facet of a broader idea, joined to it and not merged into it; the grouping is the map's and not the text's, and each aspect is described by the passages it cites.
aspect_of.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

in_theme.definition: A concept, observance, event or saying is a core concept of a major theme; the grouping is a reader's map of the text, supported by the passages cited.
in_theme.by: drafted by Claude Sonnet, approved by Doug Egge

knows.definition: A person, being or group knows another, or knows something, where the text says so.
knows.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

loves.definition: A person, being or group loves another, where the text says so.
loves.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

sees.definition: A person, being or group sees another or something done, where the text says so.
sees.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

rewards.definition: A person, being or group rewards another, where the text says it does or will.
rewards.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

forgives.definition: A person, being or group forgives another, or a wrong, where the text says it does or will.
forgives.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

reveals.definition: A person, being or group makes something known to another, where the text says so.
reveals.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

hides.definition: A person, being or group hides or keeps something from another, where the text says so.
hides.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

glorifies.definition: A person, being or group glorifies another, where the text says so.
glorifies.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

honors.definition: A person, being or group honors another, where the text says so.
honors.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

testifies_about.definition: A person, being, group or text testifies about another, where the text says so.
testifies_about.by: drafted by Claude Opus; the words approved by Doug Egge 2026-11-01

dwells_in.definition: One is in another, or dwells or remains in another, in the words the text uses; the relation says nothing beyond the verse it cites.

quotes.definition: The Berean editors note that this verse quotes that one: Matthew 4:4 quotes Deuteronomy 8:3. The editors make the link; the two verses' shared words are its evidence. Read from the other side, the earlier verse is quoted in the later.

points_to.definition: The Berean editors refer this verse, or the section it begins, to that one: in a note, or in the list of passages under a section heading. For the gospels those lists are the parallel accounts; elsewhere they are not (Isaiah 53's lists 1 Peter 2:21), so this term claims only that the editors point from one to the other, not what the two share.

alludes_to.definition: This verse takes up words or an image of that one without quoting it, as judged by a reader of both verses. Always a reading, never a statement of the text or of the editors.
alludes_to.by: drafted by Claude Opus, 2026-11-12, for the term set Doug chose (plan 8.7c); approved by Doug Egge on 2026-11-12 ('Approved')

echoes.definition: A later verse shares rare words with an earlier one, found by matching the Greek against the Hebrew's Septuagint renderings, not by reading either verse. Each link carries its grade from a hand check: "strong" was real about 5 times in 8, "likely" about 4 in 8. It does not claim that the later verse quotes the earlier or means it.
echoes.by: drafted by Claude Opus, 2026-11-12, for the term set Doug chose (plan 8.7c); approved by Doug Egge on 2026-11-12 ('Approved')

says_the_same_as.definition: The two verses say the same thing, as a model (DeepSeek Flash) judged the pair after the alignment found it: a parallel account (Matthew 4:4 and Luke 4:4, the first temptation's answer), one promise said twice (John 3:16 and 3:36), or a prophecy and its quotation (Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23).
